manual/advanced/build-and-resources.html.summary: Build and resources The default styling is defined in graph-default-style.uss, which can be found in the com.andywiecko.graphs/Runtime/Resources/ folder of the package. This style sheet is automatically attached to every created Graph object. You can override this behavior by modifying the static Graph.DefaultStyleSheet field. Since this style sheet is located in a Resources folder, it will be included automatically in the project build. If you do not want to include the default style sheet, you must handle this manually by removing it from Resources or by using a build script (for example, using AssetDatabase.MoveAsset).

manual/advanced/custom-point-style.html.title: Custom point style | UIT Graphs
manual/advanced/custom-point-style.html.summary: Custom point style As described in Plot types/Plot with points, the package provides several built-in markers for point representation. However, it is relatively easy to define a custom marker shape. In this example, we will show how to add a half-circle marker. First, you need to implement the IPointStyle interface. This interface has a single method to implement: Draw(float2, Painter2D, float). public class HalfCircleStyle : IPointStyle { public void Draw(float2 localPosition, Painter2D painter, float pointSize) { var o = pointSize; var q = localPosition; painter.BeginPath(); painter.Arc(q, o, 90, 270); painter.Fill(); painter.ClosePath(); painter.Arc(q, o, 270, 90); painter.Stroke(); } } To override a given style, you can replace one of the styles assigned to the plot by modifying plot.PointStyles[i]. var plot = graph.PlotWithPoints(Sequence.Uniform(x => x, samples: 10), theme: new() { PointSize= 15, PointWidth = 2 }); plot.PointStyles[1] = new HalfCircleStyle(); Alternatively, you can modify the static list in DefaultPointStyles to override this marker type globally for newly created graphs. DefaultPointStyles.Collection[1] = new HalfCircleStyle();

manual/advanced/custom-tics-provider.htm.title: Custom tics provider | UIT Graphs
manual/advanced/custom-tics-provider.htm.summary: Custom tics provider In the section Tutorial/Tics, you can find basic information about tic configuration for the axis. Here, we will show how to implement a custom ITicsProvider. The interface requires two elements: a Version property and a GetTics(float2) method. The Version property is used internally for optimization (e.g. caching tic labels). Increase its value whenever the tics need to be regenerated. The GetTics(float2) method returns an IReadOnlyList<Tic>. Most built-in implementations internally use a List<Tic> for caching. The method parameter represents the current axis view range, where .x is the minimum value and .y is the maximum value. Below is an example of a custom ITicsProvider that renders tics only for prime numbers1: public class TicsProviderPrimes : ITicsProvider { private static bool IsPrime(int n) => n > 1 && Enumerable.Range(2, (int)math.sqrt(n) - 1).All(i => n % i != 0); private static readonly bool[] primes = new bool[512]; static TicsProviderPrimes() { for (int i = 0; i < primes.Length; i++) primes[i] = IsPrime(i); } public int Version { get; private set; } = 0; private float2 lastRange; private readonly List<Tic> tics = new(); public TicsProviderPrimes() => lastRange = float.NaN; public IReadOnlyList<Tic> GetTics(float2 range) { if (math.all(range == lastRange)) { return tics; } tics.Clear(); var start = (int)math.floor(range.x); var end = (int)math.ceil(range.y); lastRange = range; Version++; if (end < 0 || start >= primes.Length) { return tics; } for (int i = math.max(start, 0); i <= math.min(end, primes.Length - 1); i++) { if (primes[i]) { tics.Add(new(i, i.ToString())); } } return tics; } } Then you can use this component for your graphs: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Tics = new TicsProviderPrimes(), Min = 0, Max = 20, }, }; This provider is intended for demonstration purposes only and is not recommended for production use. Additionally, the same result could be achieved more simply using the Tics.Collection utility.↩

manual/advanced/light-dark-runtime.html.title: Light, dark, runtime | UIT Graphs
manual/advanced/light-dark-runtime.html.summary: Light, dark, runtime You can define different styling behavior depending on where the graph is attached. In other words, using specific USS classes you can distinguish between editor (including dark and light mode) and runtime VisualElements. When attached to a panel, the Graph object is decorated with one of the following classes: .dark, .light, or .runtime. You can use these classes to provide context-specific styling overrides. Below you can find explicit style definitions from the default stylesheet. .graph.dark .graph-canvas { --graph-border-color: white; } .graph.light .graph-canvas { --graph-border-color: black; } .graph.runtime .graph-canvas { --graph-border-color: black; } .graph.runtime { background-color: white; } Light (Editor) Dark (Editor) Runtime

manual/advanced/override-key-elements.ht.title: Override key elements | UIT Graphs
manual/advanced/override-key-elements.ht.summary: Override key elements Sometimes it is useful to customize key elements. In this package, this can be achieved with a small workaround. For a plot whose key preview you want to override, you can add an additional plot with empty data (e.g. using Array.Empty). For such a plot, the theme can be customized independently, and a click event callback can be connected to the real plot. var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.InTopLeft } } }; var realPlot = graph.PlotWithLinesPoints(Sequence.Uniform(x => x, samples: 10), theme: new() { PointStyle = 7, PointSize = 2 }); var fakePlot = graph.PlotWithLinesPoints(Array.Empty<float2>(), "fake", theme: new() { PointStyle = 7, PointSize = 4 }); fakePlot.SetStyle(1); fakePlot.KeyElement.RegisterCallback<ClickEvent>(_ => realPlot.style.display = !fakePlot.KeyElement.Q<Label>().enabledSelf ? DisplayStyle.None : DisplayStyle.Flex ); fakePlot.KeyElement.Q<VisualElement>("StylePreview").style.width = 15; In this demo, I connected the callback, pre-styled the preview by making the point marker larger, and additionally overridden the width of the plot preview rendering, which results in a shorter line in the key.

manual/examples/area-demo.html.title: Area demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/area-demo.html.summary: Area demo Below is a simple demo showing how to use PlotWithFilledBaseline to create an area plot. var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -5, Max = 5 }, YAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 1 }, style = { width = 500, height = 300 }, Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.InTopLeft }, Grid = { Display = DisplayStyle.None }, } }; static float norm(float sigma) => math.sqrt(math.PI2 * sigma * sigma); static float gauss(float x, float mu, float sigma) => math.exp(-(x - mu) * (x - mu) / sigma / sigma) / norm(sigma); graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline( data: Sequence.Uniform(x => gauss(x, mu: 0.5f, sigma: 0.5f), samples: 200), title: "μ=0.5 σ=0.5", y0: -1e-9f // NOTE: slightly below 0f to avoid floating-point artifacts during clipping. ); graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline( data: Sequence.Uniform(x => gauss(x, mu: 2, sigma: 1), samples: 200), title: "μ=2 σ=1" ); graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline( data: Sequence.Uniform(x => gauss(x, mu: -1, sigma: 2), samples: 200), title: "μ=-1 σ=2" );

manual/examples/bar-plot-demo.html.summary: Bar plot demo Below is a simple demo showing how to use PlotWithBars to create a bar plot. var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -1, Max = 12, Tics = Tics.Manual(new Tic[] { (00, "Jan"), (01, "Feb"), (02, "Mar"), (03, "Apr"), (04, "May"), (05, "Jun"), (06, "Jul"), (07, "Aug"), (08, "Sep"), (09, "Oct"), (10, "Nov"), (11, "Dec"), }) }, YAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 13 }, Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.InTopLeft }, Grid = { Display = DisplayStyle.None }, Tics = { Direction = TicsDirection.Out, Bits = (int)(BorderBits.Left | BorderBits.Bottom) } }, style = { height = 300, width = 450 }, }; graph.PlotWithBars(new float2[] { new(0, 1), new(1, 5), new(2, 2), new(3, 1), new(4, 7), new(5, 8), new(6, 1), new(7, 7), new(8, 5), new(9, 1), new(10, 9), new(11, 11), }, width: 0.3f, anchor: BarAnchor.Right, title: "2025"); graph.PlotWithBars(new float2[] { new(0, 1 + 2), new(1, 5 - 1), new(2, 2 + 4), new(3, 1 + 0), new(4, 7 + 1), new(5, 8 - 3), new(6, 1 + 1), new(7, 7 + 1), new(8, 5 + 3), new(9, 1 + 2), new(10, 9 - 4), new(11, 11 - 7), }, width: 0.3f, anchor: BarAnchor.Left, title: "2026").SetStyle(3);

manual/examples/fibonacci-blocks-demo.ht.title: Fibonacci blocks demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/fibonacci-blocks-demo.ht.summary: Fibonacci blocks demo Below is a simple demo demonstrating how to plot Fibonacci blocks using PlotWithLines and PlotWithBoxes. var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Tics = Tics.Step(-1000, 1, 1000, formatter: _ => "") }, YAxis = { Tics = Tics.Step(-1000, 1, 1000, formatter: _ => "") }, Theme = { Grid = { DashPattern = new float[] { 1 } }, Tics = { Direction = TicsDirection.None } }, style = { height = 300 }, Title = "Fibonacci blocks" }; var boxes = new List<AABB>(); var (f0, f1) = (1f, 1f); var bounds = new AABB(0, 1); boxes.Add(bounds); for (int i = 1; i < 8; i++) { var o = math.float2(f1, 0); var (p0, p1) = (i & 3) switch { 0 => (bounds[0] - o.yx, bounds[0] + o.xy), 1 => (bounds[1], bounds[2] + o.xy), 2 => (bounds[3], bounds[3] + o.xx), 3 => (bounds[0] - o.xy, bounds[0] + o.yx), _ => throw new(), }; var box = AABB.Construct(p0, p1); boxes.Add(box); bounds = bounds.Union(box); (f0, f1) = (f1, f0 + f1); } var spiral = new List<float2>(); for (var i = 0; i < boxes.Count; i++) { var b = boxes[i]; var r = b.Max.x - b.Min.x; var center = b[((i + 2) & 3)]; var phi0 = 0.5f * math.PI * ((i + 2) & 3); const int N = 32; for (var j = 0; j <= N; j++) { var phi = phi0 + 0.5f * math.PI * j / N; math.sincos(phi, out var s, out var c); spiral.Add(center + r * math.float2(c, s)); } } graph.PlotWithLines(spiral, theme: new() { LineWidth = 2 }); graph.PlotWithBoxes(boxes, theme: new() { LineColor = Color.black, FillColor = new Color(), });

manual/examples/signal-demo.html.title: Signal demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/signal-demo.html.summary: Signal demo Below is a simple demo showing how to draw a signal over time. The chosen signal is a simple sine function with additional noise. The signal is displayed within a moving window of length 3 seconds and is sampled at a frequency of 60 Hz. The data buffer stores between 900 and 1800 of the most recent samples. private Graph graph; private List<float2> data = new(); private void Start() { graph = new() { XAxis = { Label = "time (s)" }, YAxis = { Min = -1.5f, Max = +1.5f }, style = { width = 400, height = 300 } }; graph.PlotWithLines(data, theme: new() { LineWidth = 3 } ); } private float t = 0; private float freq = 60; private float reset = float.MaxValue; private float window = 3; private int maxcount => (int)(10 * window * freq); private void Update() { var dt = Time.deltaTime; t += dt; reset += dt; if (reset < 1 / freq) { return; } reset = 0; var fx = math.sin(2 * t) + 0.5f * noise.snoise(new float2(3 * t, 0)); data.Add(new(t, fx)); graph.XAxis.Min = math.max(t - window, 0); graph.XAxis.Max = math.max(t, window); graph.Replot(); if (data.Count > maxcount) { data.RemoveRange(0, maxcount / 2); } } Warning Remember that this Graph must be included in a UI Document or a corresponding component editor to render correctly.

manual/examples/sp500-demo.html.title: S&P 500 demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/sp500-demo.html.summary: S&P 500 demo Below you can find a demo plot for the S&P 500 Index. The dataset contains 7700 data points and was obtained from https://stooq.com/. In the script, you can see how to load a simple CSV file into a C# array of float2. Additionally, the example demonstrates a simple technique for using Tics.Manual to create datetime-like plots. [SerializeField] private TextAsset csv; private void Start() { CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture; var rows = csv.text .Split('\n') .Skip(1) // skip header .Where(line => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line)) .Select(line => { var v = line.Split(','); return new { Date = v[0], Open = float.Parse(v[1]), High = float.Parse(v[2]), Low = float.Parse(v[3]), Close = float.Parse(v[4]), Volume = float.Parse(v[5]), }; }).ToArray(); var sp500 = rows.Select((i, v) => math.float2(v, 0.5f * (i.Open + i.Close))).ToArray(); var graph = new Graph { Title = "S&P 500 Index", XAxis = { Label = "Date", Tics = Tics.Manual(new Tic[] { new(1000, rows[1000].Date[..^3]), new(3000, rows[3000].Date[..^3]), new(5000, rows[5000].Date[..^3]), new(7000, rows[7000].Date[..^3]), }) }, YAxis = { Label = "Price ($)", LabelRotation = -90, Tics = Tics.Auto(4), Min = 0 }, style = { height = 300 }, }; graph.PlotWithLines(sp500, theme: new() { LineWidth = 0.5f }); }

manual/examples/stacked-area-demo.html.title: Stacked area demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/stacked-area-demo.html.summary: Stacked area demo Below is a simple demo showing how to use PlotWithFilledBaseline and PlotWithFilledCurves to create a stacked area plot. var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 1 }, YAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 1 }, style = { width = 400, height = 300} }; static float f1(float x) => 0.1f + 0.4f * x + 0.1f * math.sin(7 * math.PI * x); static float f2(float x) => 0.7f + 0.05f * x + 0.15f * math.sin(5 * math.PI * x); graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline(Sequence.Uniform(x => f1(x), samples: 10), y0: 0); graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline(Sequence.Uniform(x => f2(x), samples: 10), y0: 1); graph.PlotWithFilledCurves(SequencePair.Uniform(x => math.float2(f1(x), f2(x)), samples: 10));

manual/examples/stacked-bar-plot-demo.ht.title: Stacked bar plot demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/stacked-bar-plot-demo.ht.summary: Stacked bar plot demo Below is a simple example showing how to create a stacked bar plot using [PlotWithBoxes][plot-with-boxes]. var graph = new Graph() { XAxis = { Min = -0.5f, Max = 5.5f, Tics = Tics.Manual(new Tic[] { (0, "2021"), (1, "2022"), (2, "2023"), (3, "2024"), (4, "2025"), (5, "2026"), })}, YAxis = { Max = 25 }, Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.OutRightTop }, Tics = { Bits = (int)(BorderBits.Bottom | BorderBits.Left), Direction = TicsDirection.Out }, Grid = { Display = DisplayStyle.None }, }, }; graph.Canvas.style.backgroundColor = new Color(1, 1, 1, 0.25f); graph.Key.style.backgroundColor = new Color(1, 1, 1, 0.25f); var alice = new Dictionary<float, float> { [0] = 3, [1] = 4, [2] = 2, [3] = 7, [4] = 4, [5] = 8, }; var bob = new Dictionary<float, float> { [0] = 4, [1] = 1, [2] = 3, [3] = 3, [4] = 5, [5] = 6, }; var charlie = new Dictionary<float, float> { [0] = 2, [1] = 3, [2] = 1, [3] = 5, [4] = 3, [5] = 6, }; static List<AABB> stack(Dictionary<float, float> self, float width, params Dictionary<float, float>[] others) { var w = 0.5f * width; var result = new List<AABB>(); foreach (var (k, v) in self) { var y0 = 0f; foreach (var o in others) { y0 += o.GetValueOrDefault(k); } var box = new AABB( min: math.float2(k - w, y0), max: math.float2(k + w, y0 + v) ); result.Add(box); } return result; } graph.PlotWithBoxes(stack(alice, width: 0.5f), title: "Alice").SetStyle(3); graph.PlotWithBoxes(stack(bob, width: 0.5f, alice), title: "Bob").SetStyle(6); graph.PlotWithBoxes(stack(charlie, width: 0.5f, alice, bob), title: "Charlie").SetStyle(1);

manual/examples/trigonometric-demo.html.title: Trigonometric demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/trigonometric-demo.html.summary: Trigonometric demo In this demo, you can find a neat way of drawing basic trigonometric functions. Pay attention to how tan(x) is handled, especially how asymptotes are introduced using a dashed line, and how connections between +∞ and -∞ are avoided by inserting NaN values. Additionally, tics were manually placed at π values using a special π Unicode character. const float pi = math.PI; var graph = new Graph { style = { width = 450, height = 300 }, Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.OutRightTop } }, XAxis = { Min = -2 * pi, Max = 2 * pi, Tics = Tics.Manual(new Tic[] { (-2 * pi, "-2π"), (-pi, "-π"), (0, "0"), (pi, "+π"), (2 * pi, "+2π") }) }, YAxis = { Min = -2, Max = 2 }, }; var theme = new PlotWithLines.ThemeStyle { LineWidth = 2 }; graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => math.sin(x), samples: 1000), title: "sin(x)", theme); graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => math.cos(x), samples: 1000), title: "cos(x)", theme); static float tan(float x) => math.abs(math.cos(x)) < 0.01f ? float.NaN : math.tan(x); graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => tan(x), samples: 1000), title: "tan(x)", theme); var asymptote = new PlotWithLines.ThemeStyle { LineColor = Color.blue, LineDashPattern = new[] { 3f, 3 }, LineWidth = 1.5f, }; for (int i = -2; i <= 2; i++) { var x = (i + 0.5f) * math.PI; graph.PlotWithLines(new float2[] { new(x, -100), new(x, +100) }, theme: asymptote); }

manual/examples/wavepacket-demo.html.title: Wavepacket demo | UIT Graphs
manual/examples/wavepacket-demo.html.summary: Wavepacket demo Below is a simple demo showing how to animate a wave packet function over time within a fixed range. This example demonstrates how to replot the graph while forcing Sequence recalculation. private Graph graph; private float t; private void Start() { graph = new() { XAxis = { Min = -10, Max = 10, Label = "time (s)" }, YAxis = { Min = -1.5f, Max = +1.5f }, style = { width = 400, height = 300 } }; t = -4; var v = 3.5f; var sigma2 = 1f * 1f; var k = 5; var w = 30; var samples = 500; float gauss(float x, float t) => math.exp(-math.pow(x - v * t, 2) / 2 / sigma2); float packet(float x, float t) => gauss(x, t) * math.cos(k * x - w * t); graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => +gauss(x, t), samples)).SetStyle(0); graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => -gauss(x, t), samples)).SetStyle(0); graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => packet(x, t), samples), theme: new() { LineWidth = 2 }); } private void Update() { t += Time.deltaTime; graph.Replot(recalculateSequences: true); } Warning Remember that this Graph must be included in a UI Document or a corresponding component editor to render correctly.

manual/getting-started.html.title: Getting started | UIT Graphs
manual/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started Installation Since this is a closed-source project, pre-built packages are not provided, and the package is not published via UPM for easy updates. However, this may be introduced in the future for convenience. For now, you can install the package via a tarball or by manually copying the files. tarball manual Open the Package Manager via Window > Package Manager. Click the + button and select Install package from tarball... to install the package. The package can be installed as an embedded package. Download the files from the Unity Asset Store, then copy and extract them into the Packages/ folder of your Unity project. Quick start The core class provided by this package is Graph, which exposes methods for drawing and style customization. You can learn more about it in the Tutorial section. Below, we create an array of random float2 points and plot them using the default settings. Finally, we attach the Graph to a root VisualElement (for example, from a UI Document or a custom editor/inspector UI). var random = new Unity.Mathematics.Random(seed: 42); var data = new float2[64]; foreach (ref var i in data.AsSpan()) i = random.NextFloat2(); var graph = new Graph(); graph.PlotWithPoints(data); root.Add(graph); Demo scene The package also includes a demo scene located in the Samples~/ folder. You can manually copy these files into your Assets/ folder to explore a fully working example. Alternatively, you can open the Package Manager and import the demo using the Import button. manual/index.html.title: Manual | UIT Graphs
manual/index.html.summary: Manual This manual covers a Unity graph plotting package available on the Unity Asset Store. The package is inspired by industry-standard plotting tools such as gnuplot and matplotlib, and allows you to create graphs both at runtime and in the Unity Editor. Features Unified API for both runtime (Game View) and editor (inspectors, custom windows) graphs. Built on UI Toolkit with support for styling via .uss or C# scripts. Supported plot types: lines, points, lines points, filled area, bars, boxes, ...and more are planed (see the roadmap). Utilities for fast drawing of analytical functions. Comprehensive documentation, including tutorials and usage examples. Unity version compatibility This package is built on Unity UI Toolkit and targets modern Unity versions. The recommended Unity version is 6.3 or newer. Fully supported Partially supported1 Unsupported: Unity versions older than 6.0. Note You can send me a direct message with the Unity version you're using, and I can help verify compatibility or test it when possible. Dependencies Unity.Mathematics@1.3.3. Limitations: dashPattern is not available (introduced in Unity 6.3)↩

manual/plot-types/plot-with-bars.html.title: Plot with bars | UIT Graphs
manual/plot-types/plot-with-bars.html.summary: Plot with bars Data To plot bars, one can use PlotWithBars. This type is similar to PlotWithPoints, but instead of drawing points, it draws boxes from the baseline y0 to the corresponding points in the provided IReadOnlyList<float2> data. Additionally, you can configure the bar width and anchor. var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -1, Max = 11 }, YAxis = { Min = -7, Max = 10 }, }; var bars = new float2[] { new(0, 1), new(1, 6), new(2, 2), new(3, 9), new(4, 5), new(5, 3), new(6, -1), new(7, -6), new(8, -2), new(9, 2), new(10, 7), }; graph.PlotWithBars(bars, y0: 0, width: 0.6f, anchor: BarAnchor.Center); Similar to PlotWithPoints, NaN values are ignored. Styling This plot type has the same properties as PlotWithLines, with the addition of the FillColor property (--graph-fill-color). USS C# .my-plot { --graph-line-color: blue; --graph-line-width: 3; --graph-line-dash-pattern: "4 4"; --graph-fill-color: rgba(1.0, 0, 0, 0.5); } var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -2 * math.PI, Max = 2 * math.PI }, YAxis = { Min = -0.1f, Max = +.4f } }; var data = Sequence.Uniform(x => 0.1f * math.cos(x) + 0.15f, samples: 11); var plot = graph.PlotWithBars(data, theme: new() { LineColor = Color.blue, LineDashPattern = new float[] { 4, 4 }, LineWidth = 3, FillColor = new Color(1, 0, 0, 0.5f), });

manual/plot-types/plot-with-boxes.html.title: Plot with boxes | UIT Graphs
manual/plot-types/plot-with-boxes.html.summary: Plot with boxes Data To plot boxes, you can use PlotWithBoxes. Unlike other plot types, this plot requires an IReadOnlyList<AABB> data series. To construct a box, i.e. an AABB, you can use the constructor: var box = new AABB(min: math.float2(0, 3), max: math.float2(4, 8)); the static construction method: var box = AABB.Construct(math.float2(0, 3), math.float2(4, 8)); or other methods. See AABB in the API documentation for more details. Below is an example of a plot with randomly generated boxes. var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 50 + 4 }, YAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 30 + 4 }, Theme = { Grid = { Display = DisplayStyle.None } }, }; var random = new Unity.Mathematics.Random(seed: 42); AABB rnd() { var p = random.NextFloat2(min: 0, max: math.float2(50, 30)); var s = random.NextFloat2(min: 1, max: 8); return new(p, p + s); } var boxes = Enumerable.Range(0, 30).Select(i => rnd()).ToArray(); graph.PlotWithBoxes(boxes, theme: new() { FillColor = new(1, 0, 0, 0.1f) }); Styling This plot type has the same properties as PlotWithLines, with the addition of the FillColor property (--graph-fill-color). USS C# .my-plot { --graph-line-color: blue; --graph-line-width: 3; --graph-line-dash-pattern: "4 4"; --graph-fill-color: rgba(1.0, 0, 0, 0.5); } var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -2 * math.PI, Max = 2 * math.PI }, YAxis = { Min = -0.4f, Max = +.4f } }; static AABB ctor(float x) { var y = 0.1f * math.cos(x); return AABB.Construct( math.float2(x - 0.5f, +y + 0.15f), math.float2(x + 0.5f, -y - 0.15f) ); } var data = SequenceAABB.Uniform(x => ctor(x), samples: 11); var plot = graph.PlotWithBoxes(data, theme: new() { LineColor = Color.blue, LineDashPattern = new float[] { 4, 4 }, LineWidth = 3, FillColor = new Color(1, 0, 0, 0.5f), });

manual/plot-types/plot-with-filled-basel.title: Plot with filled baseline | UIT Graphs
manual/plot-types/plot-with-filled-basel.summary: Plot with filled baseline Data To plot the filled area between a curve and a baseline, use PlotWithFilledBaseline. Similar to PlotWithLines, the provided data must implement IReadOnlyList<float2>. You can optionally specify the baseline value y0 (by default 0f) to control the baseline. You can also specify the area to fill using FillBaseline. By default, both the areas above and below the baseline are filled. const float pi = math.PI; var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Label = "x", Min = 0, Max = 4 * pi, Tics = Tics.Manual(new Tic[] { (0, "0"), (pi, "π"), (2 * pi, "2π"), (3 * pi, "3π"), (4 * pi, "4π"), }) }, YAxis = { Label = "y", Min = -1.45f, Max = 1.45f }, style = { height = 300 }, Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.InTopRight }, Grid = { Display = DisplayStyle.None } } }; var fx = Sequence.Uniform(x => math.sin(x), samples: 200); var y0 = -0.5f; graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => y0)).SetStyle(0); graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline(fx, y0, title: "sin(x) > -0.5", theme: new() { LineColor = Color.black, FillAboveColor = Utils.ColorWithAlpha(Color.green, 0.2f), FillBelowColor = Utils.ColorWithAlpha(Color.red, 0.2f) } ); The C# example above produces the following plot: Note You can control the fill color for each section (above and below the baseline) using FillAboveColor and FillBelowColor or set the same color for both sections by providing FillColor. NaN values Similarly, one can use float.NaN to separate input data, as shown in the following example: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 3 }, YAxis = { Min = 0 }, Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.OutRightTop }, Grid = { Display = DisplayStyle.None } } }; graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline(Sequence.Uniform(x => x > 1 && x < 2 ? x * x + 1 : float.NaN, samples: 300 ), title: "x∈[1, 2]", theme: new() { LineWidth = 0 }); graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => x * x + 1), title: "x²+1", theme: new() { LineWidth = 2, LineDashPattern = new float[] { 4, 4 }, LineColor = Color.black, }); Style USS C# .my-plot { --graph-line-color: green; --graph-line-width: 3; --graph-line-dash-pattern: "4 4"; --graph-fill-above-color: red; --graph-fill-below-color: rgba(0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.5); } graph.PlotWithFilledBaseline(Sequence.Uniform(x => math.sin(x), samples: 300), theme: new() { LineColor = Color.green, LineWidth = 3, LineDashPattern = new float[] { 4, 4 }, FillAboveColor = Color.red, FillBelowColor = Utils.ColorWithAlpha(Color.blue, 0.5f), });

manual/plot-types/plot-with-filled-curve.title: Plot with filled curves | UIT Graphs
manual/plot-types/plot-with-filled-curve.summary: Plot with filled curves Data To plot the filled area between two curves, one can use PlotWithFilledCurves. In contrast to, for example, PlotWithLines, the provided data must implement IReadOnlyList<float3>. The y and z components of each float3 element correspond to the first and second data sets, respectively. var graph = new Graph { ... }; var data = new float3[] { new(0, 1, 1), new(1, 2, -1), new(2, 1.5f, -1.5f), new(3, -1, -2), new(4, 0, 2), }; var plot = graph.PlotWithFilledCurves(data); The C# example above produces the following plot: NaN values Similarly, one can use float.NaN to separate input data, as shown in the following example: var graph = new Graph { ... }; var data = new float3[] { new(0, 0, 1), new(1, 0.5f, 1.5f), float.NaN, new(2, 0.5f, 1.5f), new(4, 0, -1), }; var plot = graph.PlotWithFilledCurves(data); Styling This plot type has the same properties as PlotWithLines, with the addition of the FillColor property (--graph-fill-color). USS C# .my-plot { --graph-line-color: blue; --graph-line-width: 3; --graph-line-dash-pattern: "4 4"; --graph-fill-color: rgba(1.0, 0, 0, 0.5); } var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -2 * math.PI, Max = 2 * math.PI }, YAxis = { Min = -0.5f, Max = +.5f } }; var data = SequencePair.Uniform(x => math.float2( +0.1f * math.cos(x) + 0.15f, -0.1f * math.cos(x) - 0.15f), samples: 200 ); var plot = graph.PlotWithFilledCurves(data, theme: new() { LineColor = Color.blue, LineDashPattern = new float[] { 4, 4 }, LineWidth = 3, FillColor = new Color(1, 0, 0, 0.5f), });

manual/plot-types/plot-with-lines-points.title: Plot with lines points | UIT Graphs
manual/plot-types/plot-with-lines-points.summary: Plot with lines points Data This plot type is a combination of PlotWithLines and PlotWithPoints. See the Plot types/Plot with lines and Plot types/Plot with points sections for more details. var graph = new Graph { ... }; var data = new float2[] { ... }; graph.PlotWithLinesPoints(data); Styling It shares the same styling properties as PlotWithLines and PlotWithPoints. USS C# .my-plot { --graph-line-color: rgb(0,0,255); --graph-line-width: 4; --graph-line-dash-pattern: "7 2 4 2"; --graph-point-width: 4; --graph-point-size: 15; --graph-point-color: rgb(255,0,0); --graph-point-fill-color: rgba(0, 255, 0, 0.5); --graph-point-dash-pattern: "4 1"; --graph-point-style: 9; } var graph = new Graph { ... }; var data = new float2[] { new(0, 0), new(2, 1), new(2, 3), new(4, 2), float.NaN, new(5, 5), new(6, 1), new(7, 3), }; graph.PlotWithLinesPoints(data, theme: new() { LineColor = Color.blue, LineDashPattern = new[] {7f, 2, 4, 2}, LineWidth = 4, PointColor = Color.red, PointFillColor = Utils.ColorWithAlpha(Color.green, 0.5f), PointDashPattern = new[] { 4f, 1 }, PointSize = 15, PointStyle = (int)PointStyle.TriangleUpFilled, PointWidth = 4 });

manual/plot-types/plot-with-lines.html.title: Plot with lines | UIT Graphs
manual/plot-types/plot-with-lines.html.summary: Plot with lines Data The simplest plot available in the package is the lines plot. This type of plot simply draws lines between the provided points. To add a plot to the graph, call the PlotWithLines method and provide the data. var graph = new Graph { ... }; var data = new float2[] { new(0, 0), new(1, 2), new(2, 1), new(3, 3), new(4, 2), }; var plot = graph.PlotWithLines(data); In the above example, we used float2[] as the provided data, but it can be any type that implements IReadOnlyList (e.g. List or native collections). For analytical formulas, you can also use the Sequence. Note The graph axis will automatically adapt to the range of the provided data if not specified. You can also provide a title for the plot, which will automatically be included in the key (if enabled). var plot = graph.PlotWithLines( data: ..., title: "my data" ); // or using property: plot.Title = "my data 2"; NaN values Additionally, the data can contain float.NaN. These values will be skipped during rendering and can also be used to separate line segments. For example, this data: var data = new float2[] { new(0, 0), new(1, 0), float.NaN, new(2, 1), new(3, 1), float.NaN, new(4, 2), new(5, 2), }; will be rendered as: Warning Single points separated by NaN will not be rendered, i.e. { ..., float.NaN, new(0, 1), float.NaN, ... } Styling By default, the package defines a style palette in the USS document, and each plot (regardless of type) is assigned the next style index, i.e. USS classes .style-1, .style-2, ..., up to .style-161. In other words, when plotting multiple datasets on a graph, the plots are automatically styled according to this palette without the need for custom configuration, for example: var graph = new Graph { ... }; for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++) { var y0 = -i; graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => y0)); } will be rendered as You can manually add or remove styles using UI Toolkit methods, for example: var plot = graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => math.sin(2 * math.PI * x))); plot.RemoveFromClassList("style-1"); plot.AddToClassList("style-0"); Alternatively, you can use the SetStyle extension method: plot.SetStyle(0); You can customize the style of the line (color, dash pattern, width) using either USS or C#. USS C# If you want to customize styles via USS, you can define your own custom class and attach it to a plot object, or modify one of the predefined .style-... classes. You can use the following properties: .my-plot { --graph-line-color: white; --graph-line-width: 3; --graph-line-dash-pattern: "8 4 2 4"; } When plotting, you can override the style by providing a theme style object. Keep in mind that this object may potentially be reused in other plots if needed. graph.PlotWithLines( data: Sequence.Uniform(x => math.sin(2 * math.PI * x)), title: "sin(2π x)", theme: new() { LineColor = Color.white, LineDashPattern = new[] { 8f, 4, 2, 4, }, LineWidth = 3 } ); There is also .style-0, which is applied after the 16 basic styles. This style is reserved as a supplementary predefined style, for example for drawing asymptotes and other elements.↩

manual/plot-types/plot-with-points.html.title: Plot with points | UIT Graphs
manual/plot-types/plot-with-points.html.summary: Plot with points Data Similar to PlotWithLines, the point plotting type requires IReadOnlyList<float2> data. This method renders points within the graph view, and all NaN values are ignored. var graph = new Graph { ... }; var data = new float2[] { ... }; graph.PlotWithPoints(data); Styling Similar to PlotWithLines, the package defines a default style palette in the USS document, and each plot (regardless of type) is assigned the next style index, i.e. USS classes .style-1, .style-2, ..., up to .style-16. See Plot with Lines#Styling for details about how .style-... classes are handled. In other words, when plotting multiple graphs, the plots are automatically styled according to this palette without the need for custom configuration, for example: var graph = new Graph { ... }; for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++) { var y0 = -i; graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform(x => y0)); } will be rendered as The package provides 16 predefined marker primitives. In Advanced/Custom Point Style, you can learn how to define custom marker shapes. Similar to PlotWithLines, you can configure styling via USS or C# by predefining a theme. You can customize point size, point width (which controls the stroke line width), point style, point color (stroke), point fill color (by default using a reduced alpha of the point color), and dash pattern (stroke). USS C# .my-plot { --graph-point-width: 4; --graph-point-size: 5; --graph-point-color: rgb(0,0,255); --graph-point-fill-color: rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5); --graph-point-dash-pattern: "1 1"; --graph-point-style: 7; } var rnd = new Unity.Mathematics.Random(seed: 42); var data = new List<float2>(); for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { data.Add(rnd.NextFloat() * rnd.NextFloat2Direction()); } graph.PlotWithPoints(data, title: "my data", theme: new() { PointColor = Color.blue, PointFillColor = Utils.ColorWithAlpha(Color.red, 0.5f), PointDashPattern = new[] { 1f, 1 }, PointSize = 5, PointStyle = (int)PointStyle.CircleFilled, PointWidth = 4 }); Note You can use the PointStyle enum for a human-readable marker style definition.

manual/tutorial/axis.html.title: Axis | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/axis.html.summary: Axis Graph objects contain two axis properties: XAxis and YAxis, which are used for x and y axis configuration respectively. Both are available from the root object, for example: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { ... }, YAxis = { ... }, }; Range By default, the graph axis range is adjusted automatically based on the data provided in the plots. However, the user can fix the range from the left side, right side, or both. To configure these ranges, use the Min and Max properties. By default, both are set to null, which enables automatic scaling for the corresponding half-axis. For example, the following configuration sets the x-axis to [-2, 5] and the y-axis to [5, 6]: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -2, Max = 5 }, YAxis = { Min = 5, Max = 6 }, }; Note Pay attention to the auto tic labels. In later sections, we will learn how to customize them. Label To set up an axis label, use the Label property, for example: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Label = "x" }, YAxis = { Label = "y" }, } Alternatively, you can access the corresponding VisualElement using the Q() query. var graph = new Graph(); graph.Q

manual/tutorial/border.html.title: Border | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/border.html.summary: Border Bits Inspired by the gnuplot syntax, you can control which parts of the border are enabled. This is a simple notation that can be quite useful, especially in the future when supporting 3D plots or alternative coordinate systems such as polar plots. Bit Part 1 bottom 2 left 4 top 8 right USS C# .graph-canvas { --graph-border-bits: 3; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Border = { Bits = 1 + 2 } } }; Alternatively you can use bit notation var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Border = { Bits = 0b0011 } } }; or using custom enum var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Border = { Bits = (int)(BorderBits.Left | BorderBits.Bottom) } } }; Styling You can customize the border using a custom color, line width, or dash pattern. USS C# .graph-canvas { --graph-border-color: magenta; --graph-border-width: 2.5; --graph-border-dash-pattern: "5 2"; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Border = { Color = Color.magenta, DashPattern = new[] { 5f, 2f, }, Width = 2.5f, } } };

manual/tutorial/graph.html.title: Graph | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/graph.html.summary: Graph Basics When using this package, the only class you will typically create manually is Graph. This is the main container (VisualElement) for your plots. The hierarchy is fairly complex (see the UXML reference) because a graph contains multiple UI elements such as keys, tics, labels, and axes. Some of these elements use standard UI Toolkit styling classes and properties, which can be configured via .uss and C#. In addition, this package introduces custom properties (see the USS reference). In the tutorial, you will learn how to customize different parts of the graph when needed. The simplest graph is an empty graph with no plots. To create a graph titled "My graph" with dimensions 600x400, you can use the following: var graph = new Graph { Title = "My graph", style = { width = 600, height = 400 }, }; This creates a graph with a size of 600×400 pixels, including labels (the canvas area is automatically adjusted to account for other UI elements). Keep in mind that in some contexts, such as editor inspectors, you may prefer an auto-sized graph that adapts to the available panel width. This can be achieved by simply omitting explicit dimensions. An empty graph by default uses auto ticks and an axis range of [-1, +1]. Most graph canvas settings can be configured using the Theme 1 property. All configuration options will be discussed in later sections of this tutorial. var graph = new Graph { Title = ..., style = { ... }, XAxis = { ... }, YAxis = { ... }, Theme = { ... }, }; Editor You can create a graph and attach it to, for example, a custom editor or editor window. Below you can find an example of a user-defined MyComponent with an overridden inspector that displays an empty graph. using UnityEngine; public class MyComponent : MonoBehaviour { } using andywiecko.graphs; using UnityEditor; using UnityEditor.UIElements; using UnityEngine.UIElements; [CustomEditor(typeof(MyComponent))] public class MyComponentEditor : Editor { public override VisualElement CreateInspectorGUI() { var root = new VisualElement(); InspectorElement.FillDefaultInspector(root, serializedObject, this); var graph = new Graph(); root.Add(graph); return root; } } Runtime The simplest way to generate a graph at runtime (GameView) using this package is by creating a .uxml document and adding a Graph element to it. First, create a MyComponent.uxml file in the Assets/ folder. <ui:UXML xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:ui="UnityEngine.UIElements" xmlns:uie="UnityEditor.UIElements" noNamespaceSchemaLocation="../../UIElementsSchema/UIElements.xsd" editor-extension-mode="False"> <andywiecko.graphs.Graph style="width: 400px; height: 300px;"/> </ui:UXML> Alternatively, you can use the UI Builder to create and edit the .uxml file visually. Finally, assign this .uxml file to a UI Document component attached to a MonoBehaviour. After that, you should see the graph rendered in the GameView. The name is chosen to clearly distinguish it from Unity's built-in style property.↩

manual/tutorial/grid.html.title: Grid | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/grid.html.summary: Grid Display The graph grid is enabled by default and aligned with the tics. You can disable the grid using either USS or C#. USS C# .graph-grid { display: none; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Grid = { Display = DisplayStyle.None, } } }; Styling You can customize the grid using a custom color, line width, or dash pattern. USS C# .graph-canvas { --graph-grid-color: magenta; --graph-grid-width: 2.5; --graph-grid-dash-pattern: "5 2"; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Grid = { Color = Color.magenta, DashPattern = new[] { 5f, 2f, }, Width = 2.5f, } } };

manual/tutorial/index.html.title: Tutorial | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/index.html.summary: Tutorial In these tutorial sections you can learn about basic configuration of the Graph component. Alternatively you can follow the demos included in the Examples to learn how to configure the graph.

manual/tutorial/key.html.title: Key | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/key.html.summary: Key Position The user can use one of 21 predefined key positions to place the key automatically. Below you can find a schematic figure showing the corresponding key positions for the USS --graph-key-position property values. The graph canvas border is marked with a solid black line. Alternatively, you can configure this in C# using the KeyPosition enum (with the same names in CamelCase). USS C# .graph-canvas { --graph-key-position: in-top-right; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Key = { Position = KeyPosition.InTopRight } } }; Visibility By default, key visibility is set automatically. If a Graph contains plots with a non-null and non-empty title, the key will be rendered. Otherwise, it is hidden by default. Below you can find a table with possible key visibility settings, which can be configured via the USS --graph-key-visibility property or via C# using Graph.Theme.Key.Visibility. USS C# Description auto KeyVisibility.Auto The key is visible only if it contains visible attached elements. always KeyVisibility.Always The key is always visible, even if no elements are attached. never KeyVisibility.Never The key is never visible, even if it contains elements. manual KeyVisibility.Manual Key visibility is controlled manually using key.style.display. USS C# .graph-canvas { --graph-key-visibility: auto; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Key = { Visibility = KeyVisibility.Auto } } }; Styling Currently, all key styling can be achieved using built-in UI Toolkit properties. Check out the USS classes and default configuration: .graph-key { flex-direction: column; align-items: flex-end; border-width: 1px; margin: 6px; } .graph-key-element { flex-direction: row; margin: 1px; font-size: 12px; } .graph-key-style-preview { width: 40px; margin: 2px; } Alternatively, you can configure this through C#. Just use the Key reference: var graph = new Graph { Key = { style = { ... } } }; Keep in mind that depending on the KeyPosition, the object can be parented to different elements. Because of this, it is recommended to use graph.Key instead of querying it manually using graph.Q<Key>(). See the UXML reference for details regarding the Key element structure.

manual/tutorial/replot.html.title: Replot | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/replot.html.summary: Replot The graph should automatically repaint itself when its geometry changes (for example, when the editor width changes) or when rendering tics and other UI elements. However, if the plot data has been modified, the graph will not detect this automatically. In such cases, the user must explicitly request a replot by calling: var graph = new Graph(); graph.Replot(); You may also need to call this method manually when certain settings are changed. However, most configuration changes should trigger Replot() automatically.

manual/tutorial/sequence.html.title: Sequence | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/sequence.html.summary: Sequence Most of the plot types available in this package require data in the form of IReadOnlyList<float2>. This means you can provide data stored in standard C# arrays, lists, or native collections. Plot types keep a reference to the provided list, and by calling graph.Replot() you can refresh the plot to reflect any changes in the underlying data. For convenience, a Sequence type has been introduced. It allows you to generate collections automatically via a lambda expression, and it will also regenerate when the graph view changes. This is especially useful when working with animations (see Signal demo and Wavepacket demo), or for quickly rendering analytical functions. var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = -2, Max = 6 }, YAxis = { Min = -1.1f, Max = 1.1f } }; graph.PlotWithLines(Sequence.Uniform( x => x > 0 ? x < math.PI ? math.cos(x) : -1 : 1, samples: 500 )); See also: ISequence SequencePair SequenceAABB

manual/tutorial/styling-order.html.title: Styling order | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/styling-order.html.summary: Styling order In this package, the user has multiple ways of overriding the graph style. The priority of styling is similar to UI Toolkit elements. Custom USS properties (e.g. --graph-grid-color) do not work inline in UXML elements. However, you can include a stylesheet with overrides in UXML using <Style src="..." /> or you can define the style through C# script. The priority of style resolution is as follows (higher value = higher priority): Default style (applied automatically in the Graph constructor). USS overrides (modified manually in UXML or through UI Builder). C# scripts (e.g. using Graph.Theme).

manual/tutorial/tics.html.title: Tics | UIT Graphs
manual/tutorial/tics.html.summary: Tics You can customize tic values and formatting for each axis. This is done using the ITicsProvider interface. There are several built-in implementations that cover most common use cases. Below you will find a brief description of each of them. Additionally, you can learn how to implement a custom provider in the Advanced/Custom Tics Provider section. All default implementations can be accessed via the Tics static class. Tic Tic is a helper struct used for tics generation related to a given axis. Internally, it is essentially a tuple of float and string. var tic = new Tic(value: 1.2f, label: "1.200"); Auto Tics.AutoProvider is the default provider used for tics generation. It creates tics based on the current minimum and maximum axis values. It has one configurable parameter: prefferedCount. This parameter allows the user to control the density of tics on the axis. However, the resulting number of tics is not guaranteed, since the internal implementation assumes evenly spaced tics aligned with zero-based offsets on the axis. Use Tics.Auto(...) to create a new AutoProvider instance: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Tics = Tics.Auto(), Min = 1, Max = 3 }, YAxis = { Tics = Tics.Auto(preferedCount: 3), Min = 0, Max = 10 }, }; Collection Using the Tics.CollectionProvider, you can define specific tics at given values by providing a collection1 var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 1, Max = 3, Tics = Tics.Collection(new[] { 1, 2, 2.5f, 2.75f, 2.9f, 3f }), }, }; Step If you need uniformly distributed tics with a given step from start to end, use Tics.StepProvider: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 1, Max = 3, Tics = Tics.Step(start: 1.2f, step: 0.2f, end: 2.8f), }, }; Manual You can provide arbitrary tic labels for given values using Tics.ManualProvider: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 1, Tics = Tics.Manual(new Tic[]{ new(value: 1f / 4, label: "¼"), new(value: 2f / 4, label: "½"), new(value: 3f / 4, label: "¾"), }), }, }; Combine Using the Tics.CombineProvider, you can combine multiple ITicsProviders into a single provider. This can be especially useful when you want to mark specific constants on plots (e.g. π). There are two ways to achieve this in the API: Using an extension method, you can call provider.Combine(other) var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 0, Max = math.PI2, Tics = Tics.Auto().Combine(Tics.Manual(new[]{ new Tic(math.PI, "π") })) }, }; Using a collection-based helper, you can combine multiple providers via Tics.Combine(...) var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 0, Max = math.PI2, Tics = Tics.Combine( Tics.Auto(), Tics.Manual(new[]{ new Tic(math.PI, "π") }) ), } } String formatting You can also easily format tic strings by providing an optional formatter parameter, which is of type Func<float, string>. This option is available for the Auto, Collection, and Step providers. Below is an example using percentage formatting2: var graph = new Graph { XAxis = { Min = 0, Max = 1, Tics = Tics.Auto( preferedCount: 3, formatter: v => v.ToString("P2") ), }, }; Tics Direction You can also define the direction of tics to render them inside the canvas (in), outside the canvas (out), or on both sides (both). This can be set via USS using the values in, out, or both, or via the TicsDirection enum. You can also disable tics entirely by providing none (or TicsDirection.None). USS C# .graph-canvas { --graph-tics-direction: both; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Tics = { Direction = TicsDirection.Both } } }; Styling You can personalize tics via color, length, width, bits3, and dash pattern. USS C# .graph-canvas { --graph-tics-color: red; --graph-tics-length: 10; --graph-tics-width: 2; --graph-tics-bits: 12; --graph-tics-dash-pattern: "4 2"; } var graph = new Graph { Theme = { Border = { Bits = 0 }, Tics = { Color = Color.red, Length = 10, Width = 2, Bits = 4+8, DashPattern = new float[]{ 4, 2 }, } } }; You can provide any object that can be cast to ReadOnlySpan.↩ Learn more about .NET string formatting in the C# reference.↩ Same notation as introduced in border styling, see Tutorial/Border.↩
